children: SpaceX
shares rose 1.5% in extended trading Tuesday after the rocket launch and satellite communications company
third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded Wall Street's expectations, fueled by explosive growth in its artificial intelligence business.

The company, which went public in June, reported net income of $4.4 billion, or $0.35 a share, beating analysts' consensus estimate of $0.16 a share by $0.19 and reversing a year-earlier net loss of $1.1 billion. The earnings announcement didn't provide the year-earlier loss per share.
Revenue surged 161% to $14.6 billion from $5.6 billion a year earlier, exceeding Wall Street's estimate of $13 billion by $1.6 billion.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or ebitda, climbed 306% to $8.8 billion from $2.2 billion a year earlier. Operating income reached $2.8 billion.
Artificial intelligence drives growth
For investors, the results highlight a significant transformation in SpaceX's

business model. Once primarily known for its Falcon 9 rockets and Starlink satellite internet service, the company is increasingly generating revenue from artificial intelligence infrastructure and software. Its Super Intelligence segment accounted for more than half of quarterly revenue, suggesting that AI could become the company's largest growth engine as demand for computing capacity accelerates.

The shift also creates new questions about the sustainability of that growth. Investors will be watching whether large cloud services agreements, acquisitions and growing adoption of AI applications can support continued expansion. Meanwhile, Starlink provides recurring subscription revenue and the company's launch operations remain an important part of its broader infrastructure strategy.

Super Intelligence revenue soared 830% from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, an increase of 195% from the second quarter. The company attributed the growth to new cloud services agreements, its acquisition of Cursor and increased adoption of Grok among enterprise customers and consumers.

The segment generated $6.7 billion in additional revenue compared with the year-earlier period. The company's AI infrastructure also continued expanding, with nameplate computing capacity reaching 1.7 gigawatts as of Sept. 30.
Starlink boosts connectivity revenue

Connectivity revenue increased 69% from a year earlier to $5.2 billion, up 22% sequentially. Consumer revenue grew 57% year over year and 26% from the previous quarter, supported by continued Starlink subscriber growth.
Enterprise and government revenue rose 91% from a year earlier and 18% sequentially, reflecting growing demand for satellite connectivity among institutional customers.
The company said operating income in its Connectivity segment increased 99% from a year earlier, indicating that revenue growth is translating into improved profitability.
Starship begins generating revenue

Space revenue reached $1.8 billion, increasing 6% from a year earlier and 84% sequentially. The company completed 12 customer launches during the quarter, including NASA's mission to launch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
Another milestone was the first revenue-generating Starship mission, which delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites to the company's broadband constellation.

According to the earnings release, the satellites represented approximately 10 times the downlink capacity added by a typical Falcon 9 Starlink launch. That improvement could help the company expand broadband capacity as demand for satellite internet services grows.
Management highlights operating leverage
In commentary accompanying the earnings announcement, Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen credited the company's performance to growth across its connectivity and AI businesses.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3," Johnsen said.
He also emphasized the importance of recurring Starlink revenue, launch operations and expanding AI infrastructure in improving the company's operating leverage.

For investors, the combination of accelerating AI revenue, expanding satellite connectivity and growing profitability offers several potential drivers of future growth. The challenge will be sustaining that momentum as the company scales its computing infrastructure and invests in its next generation of spacecraft and satellites.
